categories.name: Backend & Logic Hunting
categories.blurb: Systematically audit server code for the correctness, concurrency, error-handling, and data-integrity bugs the tests didn't catch.

prompts.title: Audit the whole codebase, worst first
prompts.blurb: Systematically review the entire codebase and report every real issue, most severe first.
prompts.summary: Reviews the whole codebase end to end — purpose, then core logic, then security — and returns only real findings, tiered Critical → Low with file, problem, fix, and impact each; no praise, no filler, ordered most severe first.
prompts.body:
Audit this entire codebase systematically and report everything that's actually
wrong. Use your tools to walk the files, modules, and dependencies — review the
whole thing, not a sample.

Work in this order:
1. Understand the system first: what it's for, its main components, and how data
   and control flow through it end to end. Establish what each part is supposed to
   guarantee before judging whether it does.
2. Then scrutinize the core logic against that purpose — flawed methodology, wrong
   assumptions, incorrect algorithms, missed cases, and places a fundamentally
   better approach exists — not just surface defects.
3. Include a security pass: input validation and trust boundaries, authentication
   and authorization, data handling and exposure, dependencies and known
   advisories, and the common vulnerability classes.

Report only real findings — no "looks good", no praise, no restating what the code
does. Categorize each by severity:
- CRITICAL: bugs, security holes, crashes, data loss, fundamental logic errors.
- HIGH: correctness bugs, performance problems, serious maintainability hazards.
- MEDIUM: inconsistencies, suboptimal patterns, missing edge cases.
- LOW: minor cleanups and small clarity wins.

For each finding give: file and line(s) → the problem stated precisely → a concrete
fix → the impact if left as-is. Where you can, prove it: name the input or
condition that triggers it, and mark findings you confirmed by tracing the code
apart from ones you merely suspect. Order the whole report most severe first.

Be concise and actionable. Don't invent issues to fill a tier — if a severity
level is empty, say so and move on.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Audit the codebase for logic bugs
prompts.blurb: Hunt for functions that return wrong results in some cases.
prompts.summary: Reads the logic-bearing functions and reports correctness bugs — bad conditionals, off-by-ones, overflow, missed edge cases — each with a triggering input, a concrete fix, and a severity ranking.
prompts.body:
Audit this codebase for logic and correctness bugs — the kind that return wrong
results in some cases and slip past the tests. Use your tools to read the code, and
concentrate on the functions that carry real logic: parsing, calculation, state
transitions, and non-trivial conditionals.

For each one, be adversarial and specific:
1. State in one sentence what it's supposed to guarantee. Where that conflicts with
   how it's actually called, flag the gap.
2. Hunt concrete defects: off-by-one and boundary errors, wrong operator or
   comparison, inverted conditions, early returns that skip cleanup, mutation of
   shared or aliased state, integer overflow or precision loss, wrong default or
   fallthrough, and unhandled branches.
3. Enumerate the edge cases that matter — empty, single, maximal, negative or zero,
   null, duplicate, unsorted, unicode, very large, malformed — and for each predict
   what the code actually does versus what it should.
4. Report each finding as: file and line → what's wrong → an input that triggers it
   → the corrected behavior → severity (rank a silent wrong result above a crash
   above a cosmetic issue).

Where you can, prove a finding by tracing the triggering input through the code or
writing a quick failing test, and mark confirmed bugs apart from suspected ones.
Point to exact lines rather than rewriting broadly, and don't invent problems to
look thorough.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Audit error handling & failure paths
prompts.blurb: Find swallowed errors, wrong recovery, and failure paths that do the wrong thing.
prompts.summary: Traces what runs when things go wrong — swallowed or mislabeled errors, lost context, panics on bad input, broken retries and cleanup — and gives the correct propagation or recovery for each, ranked by severity.
prompts.body:
Audit how this codebase handles errors and failure — not the happy path, the paths
that run when something goes wrong. Use your tools to read the error handling,
fallbacks, retries, and cleanup code.

Look for:
1. Swallowed or hidden failures: errors caught and ignored, logged-and-continued
   when they should stop, or flattened into a success or a default that masks the
   problem.
2. Wrong or lossy propagation: errors that lose their context or cause as they
   bubble up, get remapped to the wrong type or status, or surface a message that
   misleads the caller.
3. Crashes on bad input: unwrap/panic/assert, unchecked indexing, casts, and
   division that a malformed or extreme input can blow up.
4. Broken recovery: retries without backoff or idempotency, fallbacks that fire on
   the wrong condition, cleanup that doesn't run on the error path, and partial
   failures that leave state half-updated.
5. The "this can't fail" assumptions that eventually do — external calls, parsing,
   IO, and concurrency treated as infallible.

For each: file and line → what goes wrong when it fails → the correct handling
(propagate with context, fail closed, validate first, make cleanup unconditional)
→ severity. Prove the crash or the swallow with a triggering input where you can,
and separate confirmed findings from suspected ones.

Don't invent issues to look thorough. If a category is empty, say so and move on. No praise, no restating what the code does.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Audit the write paths for data corruption
prompts.blurb: Find writes that land wrong, stale, or duplicated data in the DB, cache, or state.
prompts.summary: Maps every write path and finds the ones that can persist wrong, stale, or duplicated data, then proposes an invariant-enforcing guard and a query to find already-corrupted rows.
prompts.body:
Audit this codebase for data-integrity bugs — writes that land wrong, stale,
duplicated, or inconsistent values in the database, cache, or persistent state.
Use your tools to map the write paths and read them.

Trace it end to end:
1. Map every code path that can write or mutate persisted data — include
   background jobs, retries, migrations, cache refreshes, and concurrent requests,
   not just the obvious handlers.
2. For each writer, work out under what input or timing it would produce a bad
   value. Look hard at partial failures, missing transactions, non-idempotent
   retries, a race between read and write, a wrong WHERE or key, and cache/DB
   divergence (one updated, the other not).
3. Call out the highest-risk writers and the exact condition that triggers the
   corruption, ranked by severity.
4. For each, propose a guard that makes the invariant impossible to violate (a
   transaction, unique constraint, idempotency key, optimistic-lock version, or
   single-writer ownership) rather than just patching the symptom.
5. Suggest a query or check to find any already-corrupted records so they can be
   repaired.

Where the schema or transaction boundaries aren't obvious in the code, read the
migrations and schema to confirm them rather than guessing.

Don't invent issues to look thorough. If a category is empty, say so and move on. No praise, no restating what the code does.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Hunt for race & concurrency bugs
prompts.blurb: Find shared state, async, threads, or locks behaving wrong under concurrency.
prompts.summary: Inspects concurrent code for races, deadlocks, lost updates, and visibility bugs, proving each with a concrete interleaving and proposing the minimal synchronization fix.
prompts.body:
Audit this codebase for concurrency bugs — races, deadlocks, lost updates, and
visibility issues. Use your tools to find the code that runs concurrently
(threads, async tasks, workers, shared caches or connections) and read it.

Analyze it rigorously:
1. Identify every piece of state shared across concurrent execution and classify
   each as safe or unsafe to touch without synchronization.
2. For each unsafe access, describe a specific interleaving (T1 does X, then T2
   does Y, then T1 does Z) that produces a wrong result, a lost update, or a
   crash.
3. Check for deadlock and lock-ordering hazards: do any two paths acquire the
   same locks in different orders? Is any lock held across an await or blocking
   call?
4. Check atomicity assumptions: read-modify-write sequences that look atomic but
   aren't, and check-then-act gaps.
5. Recommend the minimal correct fix per issue (narrow the critical section,
   reorder locks, use an atomic, make state immutable, or hand off via a channel)
   and call out any fix that would hurt throughput.

Show the bad interleaving explicitly — that's the proof — and rank findings by
severity. Where the concurrency or memory model isn't clear from the code, state
the assumption you're reasoning under and flag it.

Don't invent issues to look thorough. If a category is empty, say so and move on. No praise, no restating what the code does.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Hunt resource leaks & unbounded growth
prompts.blurb: Find leaked connections, handles, tasks, and memory that grows without bound.
prompts.summary: Tracks acquired resources and accumulating state to find what never gets released or bounded — connections, handles, tasks, locks, transactions, caches, buffers — with the leak condition and the fix for each.
prompts.body:
Audit this codebase for resource leaks and unbounded growth — things acquired but
never released, or that accumulate without limit until the process degrades. Use
your tools to find where resources are opened and where state accumulates, and read
those paths.

Track each resource from acquisition to release:
1. Handles and connections: files, sockets, DB connections, pooled clients —
   acquired on every path but released on only some, especially on the error or
   early-return path.
2. Concurrency primitives: tasks or threads spawned and never joined or cancelled,
   locks taken and not released on every exit, channels never closed.
3. Transactions and sessions: opened and not committed or rolled back on failure.
4. Unbounded growth: caches, maps, queues, and buffers that only ever grow; result
   sets and reads with no limit; retained references that prevent reclamation.
5. Lifetime mismatches: a resource outliving — or dying before — what depends on it.

For each: file and line → the path where it leaks or grows unbounded → the fix
(scope-based release or RAII, an eviction bound or TTL, pagination, an explicit
close on every path) → severity by how fast it bites under real load. Where you
can, name the sequence that reproduces the growth.

Don't invent issues to look thorough. If a category is empty, say so and move on. No praise, no restating what the code does.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Pressure-test the API surface
prompts.blurb: Pressure-test every endpoint's inputs, outputs, errors, and failure modes.
prompts.summary: Reviews each endpoint's validation, output shape, error codes, idempotency, and authorization, returning a prioritized issue → why-it-bites → fix list with the genuinely dangerous ones called out.
prompts.body:
Review the HTTP API in this codebase against the inputs and failure modes
it'll actually meet in production. Use your tools to find the
route handlers and their request/response types and read them.

For each endpoint, go through it as a careful API reviewer:
1. Inputs: for every field, check validation, type coercion, bounds, required
   versus optional, and what happens on missing, extra, malformed, or oversized
   values. Flag anything that trusts the caller.
2. Outputs: is the success shape consistent and stable? Does it leak internal
   details (stack traces, internal ids, PII)? Are nullable fields documented?
3. Errors: map each failure to the right status code and a useful, non-leaky
   error body. Find paths that can 500 on bad input that should be 4xx.
4. Semantics: is it idempotent where it should be? What happens on retry,
   double-submit, or partial failure mid-write? Any race between check and act?
5. Boundaries: pagination limits, timeouts, rate limits, large payloads, and
   authorization gaps (can caller A act on caller B's resource?).

Output a prioritized list per endpoint: issue → why it bites in production → the
fix. Call out the one or two that are genuinely dangerous versus nice-to-have.

Don't invent issues to look thorough. If a category is empty, say so and move on. No praise, no restating what the code does.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

categories.name: Frontend & UI
categories.blurb: Audit layout, state, rendering, and accessibility across the UI without flailing at CSS.

prompts.title: Audit the UI for layout fragility
prompts.blurb: Find layout and CSS that misaligns, overflows, or sizes wrong.
prompts.summary: Diagnoses layout and CSS fragility from first principles and gives the smallest correct fix for each, explaining the box-model mechanism behind it so the next one is obvious.
prompts.body:
Audit the UI in this codebase for layout fragility and CSS bugs — things that
misalign, overflow, collapse, or size wrong. Use your tools to read the markup and
stylesheets; if I've described a specific symptom, start there.

Diagnose from first principles, not by changing CSS at random:
1. For each issue, explain which layout system governs it (normal flow, flexbox,
   grid, absolute or fixed positioning, float) and what the box model is doing —
   including `box-sizing`, margins and margin collapse, and any implicit
   min-content sizing.
2. Pinpoint the specific rule or missing rule causing it, and explain the
   mechanism (for example, "the flex item has min-width auto, so it refuses to
   shrink below its content and overflows").
3. Propose the smallest CSS change that would fix the cause, and say what it
   changes and why. Do not apply it. Avoid `!important`, magic pixel values, and
   stacking hacks unless you justify them.
4. Note side effects the fix could have on siblings, other breakpoints, or
   different content lengths.
5. Flag layout that's fragile even where it isn't visibly broken yet.

Prefer explanations that teach the underlying rule, so the next one is obvious.

Don't invent issues to look thorough. If a category is empty, say so and move on. No praise, no restating what the code does.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

prompts.title: Audit UI state & re-render logic
prompts.blurb: Find stale UI, missing updates, infinite loops, and components that won't re-render.
prompts.summary: Traces UI state flow to find stale values, missing updates, and render loops, naming the exact line and the timing that produces each, then the minimal correct fix.
prompts.body:
Audit the UI state management in this codebase for re-render and data-flow bugs —
stale values, missing updates, infinite render loops, unexpected resets, and
double-fires. Use your tools to read the components and the state they share.

Reason about the data flow:
1. For the stateful areas, trace each piece of state's lifecycle: where it's
   declared, every place it's read, and every place it's written. Map the path
   from event → state change → re-render → DOM.
2. Identify defect classes: mutating state in place instead of replacing it; stale
   closures capturing an old value; derived state stored instead of computed;
   effects with wrong or missing dependencies; keys causing remounts; updates
   batched or fired in the wrong order; identity changes (a new object or array
   each render) triggering loops.
3. Point at the exact line where a wrong assumption lives and explain the timing
   that produces the symptom.
4. Give the minimal correct fix, preferring deriving over storing and a single
   source of truth over synchronized copies.
5. Flag nearby footguns that will cause the next bug.

If the framework's update model matters to a conclusion, state which version or
behavior you're assuming.

Don't invent issues to look thorough. If a category is empty, say so and move on. No praise, no restating what the code does.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Accessibility audit of the components
prompts.blurb: Find keyboard and screen-reader blockers and the exact markup change.
prompts.summary: Audits components against real assistive-tech use — semantics, keyboard, screen-reader naming, forms, contrast — and returns a table of issues with the exact markup or ARIA change, blockers first.
prompts.body:
Audit the UI components in this codebase for accessibility and give concrete,
correct fixes — not a generic checklist. Use your tools to read the markup and the
behavior around it.

Evaluate against how real assistive tech uses each component:
1. Semantics: is the right native element used for each role? Name the correct
   native element for any `div` or `span` button/link/input impostors, or, only
   where unavoidable, the correct ARIA role. Flag redundant or wrong ARIA.
2. Keyboard: can every interactive element be reached and operated with the
   keyboard alone? Check tab order, focus visibility, Enter/Space/Escape/arrow
   handling, and focus management for anything that opens or closes (modals,
   menus, disclosures).
3. Screen reader: does each control have an accessible name? Are state changes
   (expanded, selected, loading, errors) announced? Are decorative icons hidden
   and meaningful ones labeled?
4. Forms: are inputs associated with labels, errors programmatically linked, and
   required or invalid states conveyed without relying on color alone?
5. Contrast and motion: call out any color-only signals or unguarded motion.

Output a table: file → issue → WCAG concern in plain terms → exact markup or
attribute change. Prioritize blockers (unusable by keyboard or screen reader)
over polish.

Don't invent issues to look thorough. If a category is empty, say so and move on. No praise, no restating what the code does.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

prompts.title: Audit responsive & cross-browser resilience
prompts.blurb: Find UI that breaks at certain widths, on mobile, or in a specific browser.
prompts.summary: Finds where the UI assumes a fixed width or a desktop engine and recommends content-driven fixes over more breakpoints, plus a short widths × browsers matrix to verify them.
prompts.body:
Audit this codebase's UI for responsive and cross-browser fragility — layouts that
break at certain widths, on mobile, or in a specific engine. Use your tools to
read the markup and CSS.

Review for resilience:
1. Find where layout assumes a fixed width, a hover that doesn't exist on touch, a
   viewport-unit quirk, or content shorter or longer than the design assumed.
2. Check the breakpoint strategy: are breakpoints driven by content needs or
   guessed device sizes? Identify the width ranges where things actually fall
   apart and explain why.
3. Flag cross-engine hazards: `100vh` on mobile, flex or grid gaps, sticky and
   positioning quirks, font rendering, date and number input differences, and any
   property needing a fallback for older targets.
4. Recommend fixes that scale with content (intrinsic sizing, `clamp()`, `minmax`,
   container-aware layout) over more hard-coded breakpoints.
5. Give a short manual test matrix (widths × browsers) to verify the fixes.

Be concrete about which property and line causes each break, and state the target
browsers and breakpoints you're assuming.

Don't invent issues to look thorough. If a category is empty, say so and move on. No praise, no restating what the code does.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

categories.name: Code Review & Refactoring
categories.blurb: Get a rigorous review of the current change, or restructure code safely without altering behavior.

prompts.title: Rigorous review of the current change
prompts.blurb: Review the working diff the way a demanding senior engineer would.
prompts.summary: Reads the working diff and reviews intent, correctness, design, risk, and test coverage, returning findings grouped Blocking / Should-fix / Nit with file:line and a concrete suggestion.
prompts.body:
Review the current change in this repository the way a demanding, fair senior
engineer reviews a pull request — substance, not style nits a linter would catch.
Use your tools to get the diff (the uncommitted changes, or this branch against
its base) and read the surrounding code it touches. If there is no uncommitted
change and no branch-vs-base diff, say so and stop. Do not invent a review.

Structure your review:
1. Intent check: in one sentence, what does this change actually do? Infer the
   goal if it isn't stated, and say you inferred it. Call out scope creep or
   unrelated edits.
2. Correctness: hunt for real bugs introduced or exposed — edge cases, error
   paths, off-by-ones, concurrency, resource leaks, and broken invariants. Tie
   each to a concrete failing scenario.
3. Design: is this the right place and shape for the change? Note leaky
   abstractions, duplicated logic that should be shared, or shared logic that
   should be duplicated. Suggest a simpler structure only if it's clearly net
   positive.
4. Risk and blast radius: what could this break elsewhere? Backward compatibility,
   migrations, performance, security, observability.
5. Tests: are the right cases covered? Name the missing test that would have
   caught the most likely regression.

Group findings as [Blocking] / [Should fix] / [Nit], each with file and line and a
concrete suggestion. If something is fine, say so — don't invent problems to look
thorough.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Refactor without changing behavior
prompts.blurb: Restructure messy code while provably preserving its observable behavior.
prompts.summary: Restructures messy code in small, individually behavior-preserving steps — and applies them — after agreeing the observable contract up front and verifying it with the existing tests.
prompts.body:
Refactor messy code in this codebase to be cleaner WITHOUT changing its observable
behavior. Behavior preservation is the hard requirement. Use your tools to read
the target before touching it; if I haven't named one, pick the worst offender you
find and note the runners-up.

Proceed carefully:
1. First, summarize the current observable behavior, including edge cases and side
   effects, so the contract being preserved is explicit. Call out any behavior
   that looks accidental, and preserve it by default unless it's clearly a bug.
2. Identify the specific smells worth fixing (duplication, deep nesting, long
   parameter lists, unclear names, mixed responsibilities) and the ones not worth
   touching right now.
3. Plan the refactor as a sequence of small, individually safe steps, each
   behavior-preserving on its own so it can be reviewed and reverted piecewise.
   Do not apply the steps until I grant permission.
4. Keep public signatures stable unless I approve a change. No new features, no
   "while I'm here" fixes.
5. After permission, verify equivalence: run the existing tests that cover this,
   and add a characterization test first if coverage is thin.

If any step would change behavior to clean things up, stop and flag it as a
separate decision rather than folding it in silently.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Audit organization and plan cleanup
prompts.blurb: Review the whole repo layout and report cleanup opportunities.
prompts.summary: Audits the entire codebase organization in read-only mode, prioritizes low-effort cleanup, and reports secrets, settings, oversized files, and stale docs — a plan only, no file writes.
prompts.body:
Audit this codebase's organization in read-only mode and produce a cleanup
plan. Do not move, rename, delete, or edit any file. Everything is a plan
for a human to review, not an action for you to take. Use your tools to walk
every file and directory; review the whole thing, not a sample.

Work in this order:
1. Understand the system first: what it's for, its main components, and how
   the pieces relate. Map the current directory layout and note where files
   actually live versus where they logically belong.
2. Produce a cleanup plan optimized for minimal effort, not perfection. This
   is a tidy-up, not a rewrite — no refactors, no renaming for taste, no
   restructuring that forces broad import changes. Order the plan biggest
   wins first: each item should state the change, the effort (small/medium/
   large), the payoff, and what references (imports, scripts, CI, docs)
   would need updating. A reader should be able to stop halfway down the
   list and still have captured most of the value. As a reference point, a
   well-organized project looks roughly like this (adapt to this project's
   language and conventions — do not impose this layout):

   project/
   ├── src/            # application code, grouped by feature or layer
   ├── tests/          # mirrors src/ structure
   ├── config/         # non-secret settings: rates, thresholds, flags
   ├── scripts/        # one-off and operational scripts
   ├── docs/           # documentation
   ├── .env            # secrets only — gitignored
   ├── .env.example    # documents required env vars with placeholders
   ├── .gitignore
   ├── AGENTS.md
   └── README.md

3. Secrets pass (report only): find every token, API key, password, or
   credential living in config files, .json files, or source code. For each,
   report where it lives and plan its move to .env with an environment-
   variable read, plus a .env.example entry. Do not move anything yourself.
   Flag any secret already committed to git history for rotation — moving it
   later is not enough.
4. Settings pass (report only): assess how service configuration — rates,
   thresholds, limits, feature flags, tunables — is organized. Plan how to
   consolidate it into a clear, consistent location and format, and note
   dead or duplicated config. Config is for settings; .env is for secrets —
   the plan must keep the two separate.
5. File-size pass (report only): list every file over 1500 lines with its
   line count. Do not split, edit, or restructure these files. Just tell
   the user these files are unusually large and should probably be broken
   down, and suggest natural seams if obvious ones exist.
6. Docs pass (report only): note whether AGENTS.md, README, or similar
   agent/onboarding docs are missing, stale, or contradict the code as it
   is today. Propose what to update. Do not write those files.

Report only real findings — no praise, no restating what the code does.
Structure the output as: (a) the prioritized cleanup plan, biggest wins
first; (b) secrets found and rotation flags; (c) oversized files; (d) any
file you couldn't confidently categorize — list it, don't guess. If a pass
turns up nothing, say so and move on.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Untangle a god function / module
prompts.blurb: Decompose one giant function or class that does too much.
prompts.summary: Inventories the responsibilities of an overgrown unit, proposes a clean decomposition along its natural seams, sequences safe extraction steps, and carries out the first one as a worked example.
prompts.body:
Find an overgrown function, class, or module in this codebase that does too many
things, and decompose it into something reasonable. Use your tools to read it and
its callers; if I've pointed at one, use that.

Do this:
1. Inventory every distinct responsibility it currently has — a bulleted set of
   "this code is responsible for X." Note where responsibilities are interleaved
   rather than separated.
2. Identify the natural seams: where data flows from one concern to the next, and
   the hidden dependencies (shared mutable state, ordering assumptions, side
   effects) that make splitting risky.
3. Propose a decomposition: the units it should become, each with a single clear
   responsibility and a small interface. Show the boundaries and how data crosses
   them.
4. Sequence the extraction so each step is small and safe and the code keeps
   working after every step. Identify the riskiest seam and how to de-risk it
   (characterization tests first, for example).
5. Propose the first extraction in full as a worked example. Do not apply it
   until I grant permission.

Optimize for "the next reader understands it in 30 seconds," not cleverness or
maximum abstraction. Don't over-engineer — flag what's fine as-is.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Naming & API ergonomics pass
prompts.blurb: Make names and interfaces clear so the code reads itself.
prompts.summary: Flags names that mislead and signatures that are easy to misuse, and proposes concrete, convention-matching renames with rationale — separating real confusion from taste, and noting ripple cost.
prompts.body:
Do a naming and interface ergonomics pass over this codebase (or the area I name)
so the code reads itself without comments. Use your tools to read the functions,
types, and public surfaces.

For each name and signature:
1. Flag names that lie, mislead, or under-describe — booleans that aren't clearly
   yes/no, vague nouns (`data`, `info`, `manager`, `helper`), units or meaning
   hidden (`timeout` in what? `size` of what?), and abbreviations that cost more
   than they save.
2. Flag interface friction: parameters easy to pass in the wrong order, boolean
   flags that should be enums, primitive obsession, functions that do something
   surprising relative to their name, and return types that force the caller to
   guess.
3. Propose concrete renames and signature changes, with a one-line rationale each.
   Keep them consistent with the codebase's existing conventions — match existing
   patterns rather than importing new ones.
4. Distinguish "genuinely confusing" from "personal-taste nit" so I can ignore the
   latter.
5. If a rename ripples to many call sites, note that cost so I can weigh it.

Prefer fewer, higher-impact changes over renaming everything.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

categories.name: Testing & QA
categories.blurb: Design test plans, write the cases that actually catch bugs, and find the gaps in coverage.

prompts.title: Build a test plan from the code
prompts.blurb: Produce a thorough, prioritized test plan for a feature or change.
prompts.summary: Turns a feature into a prioritized test plan — explicit and implicit requirements, cases by category with expected results, and an "if you only test five things" shortlist ranked by risk.
prompts.body:
Build a thorough test plan for the feature or change at hand. I want the cases
that actually matter, prioritized, not an exhaustive dump. Use your tools to read
the relevant code so the plan reflects what's really there; if the feature isn't
in the codebase yet, build the plan from whatever description is available and
state what you assumed.

Produce:
1. A short list of the explicit requirements, plus the IMPLICIT ones the code
   assumes but doesn't state (auth, permissions, limits, error handling,
   concurrency, idempotency). Flag any requirement that's ambiguous and needs a
   decision before testing.
2. Test cases by category: happy path, boundary and edge inputs, invalid inputs,
   error and failure paths, state and permission variations, and integration
   points. For each: precondition → action → expected result.
3. The nastiest realistic cases — the ones a rushed developer would miss (empty or
   huge inputs, concurrent actions, partial failures, retries, timezones, unicode,
   network loss mid-operation).
4. Which cases warrant automated tests versus one-time manual checks, and at which
   level (unit, integration, e2e).
5. A prioritized "if you only test five things" shortlist ranked by risk ×
   likelihood.

Where behavior is ambiguous, state the assumption you're testing against and flag
it as a decision to confirm rather than guessing silently.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Write tests for the cases that break things
prompts.blurb: Generate sharp tests targeting edge cases, not just the happy path.
prompts.summary: Writes and runs sharp tests aimed at the inputs most likely to break the code, deriving cases from the input space rather than the happy path, in the project's existing framework and idiom.
prompts.body:
Propose tests that target the cases most likely to break the code at hand — not
three happy-path tests, the ones that find bugs. Use your tools to read the target
code and the existing test suite, and match its framework and style.

Approach:
1. First, state the contract you're testing to: inputs, outputs, side effects, and
   invariants. If the contract is unclear for some input, list it as an open
   question rather than guessing the assertion.
2. Derive cases from the input space, not the implementation: boundaries (0, 1,
   max, max+1), empty, null, or missing, negative, duplicate, unsorted, very
   large, malformed, and unusual-but-valid (unicode, whitespace, mixed types).
3. Cover behavior, not lines: error paths and exceptions, idempotency, ordering,
   and any documented guarantee. Include at least one test that would fail if a
   plausible future "optimization" broke the contract.
4. For each case, specify a test name that states the case
   ("returns_empty_when_input_is_empty"), arrange/act/assert structure, and one
   logical assertion focus. Do not write the files until I grant permission.
5. Call out any case you suspect is a real bug (where the expected value is
   uncertain) so I can decide the intended behavior.

Keep tests deterministic — no reliance on real time, network, or ordering. After
permission, write them, run them, and report what passes.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Find untested branches & coverage gaps
prompts.blurb: Existing tests pass but you suspect they miss real risk.
prompts.summary: Separates what the tests truly assert from what they merely touch, surfaces high-risk uncovered paths and weak/over-mocked tests, and lists the specific tests to add, ranked by the risk they retire.
prompts.body:
My tests pass, but passing tests aren't the same as tested code. Find the coverage
gaps that matter in this codebase — where a real bug could hide and no test would
notice. Use your tools to read the code and its existing tests (and a coverage
report if you can generate one).

Analyze:
1. Map what the existing tests actually exercise versus what they merely touch.
   Identify branches, error paths, and conditions with NO meaningful assertion
   behind them.
2. Find the high-risk uncovered paths: error handling, fallbacks, edge
   conditions, and the "this should never happen" branches that eventually do.
3. Spot weak tests masquerading as coverage: tests that assert nothing meaningful,
   over-mock the thing they claim to verify, or would still pass if the logic were
   broken. Name them.
4. Identify behavior coupled across units where a unit test passes but the
   integration would fail — and say where an integration test is the right tool
   instead of more unit tests.
5. Give a prioritized list of specific tests to add, ranked by the risk they
   retire, each with the exact scenario it should assert.

Don't chase a coverage percentage — chase the cases whose failure would actually
hurt.

Don't invent issues to look thorough. If a category is empty, say so and move on. No praise, no restating what the code does.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

categories.name: Performance & Optimization
categories.blurb: Find the real bottleneck with evidence before you optimize, then make a change you can measure.

prompts.title: Optimize from a profile, not a hunch
prompts.blurb: Find the actual bottleneck with evidence before changing anything.
prompts.summary: Insists on a profile or measurement first, identifies the dominant cost from the numbers, and proposes the highest-leverage change ordered by win-per-effort with a before/after check.
prompts.body:
Something in this codebase is too slow and I want to fix the bottleneck that
actually matters, not the one I assume. Hold me to evidence. Use your tools to
read the relevant code, but don't optimize from reading alone.

Guide me:
1. Before changing anything, tell me what to measure to locate the bottleneck and
   how — the specific profile, trace, or timing breakdown that will show where the
   time or allocations actually go. Insist on this first; if you can run or
   suggest the exact command, do.
2. Once there are numbers, identify the dominant cost and explain why it's
   expensive (algorithmic complexity, IO and round-trips, contention,
   serialization, allocation, cache misses).
3. Propose the highest-leverage change for that dominant cost, with an estimate of
   the expected win and the effort and risk. Order options by win-per-effort.
4. Warn me away from micro-optimizations that won't move the needle given the
   profile.
5. Define how we'll confirm the improvement: the same measurement, before versus
   after, plus a check that correctness and other metrics didn't regress.

Refuse to optimize from a hunch: if there's no measurement yet, the first step is
to produce one. Name exactly what to profile and how before proposing any change.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Find the slow query / N+1
prompts.blurb: Hunt the database access for slow queries, N+1, and missing indexes.
prompts.summary: Finds N+1 patterns and expensive queries, says exactly what EXPLAIN to run and which index to add (and its write-time cost), ranked by leverage with a before/after measurement.
prompts.body:
Database access in this codebase is slow and I suspect query problems — slow
queries, N+1 patterns, missing indexes, or over-fetching. Use your tools to find
the queries and ORM calls and the code that issues them, then read them.

Analyze:
1. Identify N+1 patterns: a query inside a loop, or per-record lazy loads that
   should be a single batched or joined query. Quote the offending code with its
   location.
2. For each expensive query, walk what the engine must do: which indexes it can
   use, where it'll do a full scan or sort, and whether the WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER
   BY columns are indexed. Tell me the exact EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE to run and
   what to look for.
3. Flag over-fetching (selecting columns or rows that get discarded), missing
   pagination, and unbounded result sets.
4. Recommend fixes in order of leverage: query or JOIN restructuring, the specific
   index to add (with column order and why), batching, or caching — and note the
   write-time and storage cost of any index.
5. Give the measurement that proves it: before/after timing or query count.

Don't add indexes blindly — justify each against the queries that will use it.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Reduce memory / allocation pressure
prompts.blurb: Cut high memory use, GC pressure, or allocation churn in a hot path.
prompts.summary: Pinpoints per-iteration allocations and retained memory on the hot path and proposes impact-ordered fixes (reuse, pre-size, stream, borrow), with how to measure the difference.
prompts.body:
Something in this codebase uses more memory or allocates more than it should —
high RSS, GC pressure, or a slow hot loop from churn. Use your tools to find the
hot path and its data structures and read them. Find the waste without hurting
clarity needlessly.

Examine:
1. Identify allocations and retained memory on the hot path: temporary objects per
   iteration, copies that could be borrows or views, repeated buffer growth,
   boxing, and intermediate collections that could be streamed.
2. Distinguish "allocated once" from "allocated per call or iteration" — the
   latter is where the pressure is. Quote those lines.
3. Look at data-structure choices: oversized or wrong containers, storing more
   than needed, duplicated data that could be shared or interned, and capacity not
   pre-sized when the size is known.
4. Propose changes ordered by impact: reuse or pool buffers, pre-size, stream
   instead of materialize, borrow instead of clone, choose a tighter type — and
   flag any that trade meaningful readability for the win.
5. Tell me how to measure the difference (allocation profiler, heap snapshot, peak
   RSS) before and after.

Don't sacrifice correctness or readability for a win the workload size makes
irrelevant — say when an optimization isn't worth it.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

categories.name: Security Review
categories.blurb: Threat-model a feature and audit the codebase for the vulnerability classes that actually get exploited.

prompts.title: Threat-model a feature
prompts.blurb: Think through how a feature could be abused before shipping it.
prompts.summary: Walks an attacker through the feature's entry points and enumerates concrete abuse cases by class, rated impact × likelihood, with the specific mitigation and where in the flow it belongs.
prompts.body:
Threat-model a feature before it ships — I want to know how it gets abused, not a
generic OWASP recital. If the feature lives in this codebase, use your tools to
read it; if it's still an idea, ask me to describe it and its trust boundaries
first.

Work it through:
1. Identify the assets at risk (data, money, accounts, compute, reputation) and
   who would want them. Sketch the attacker profiles that realistically apply.
2. Map the trust boundaries and entry points: every place untrusted input enters
   and every privileged action it can reach.
3. For each entry point, enumerate concrete abuse cases — walk an attacker's
   steps. Cover the classes that fit: injection, broken authn/authz (especially
   horizontal and vertical privilege escalation and IDOR), SSRF, insecure
   deserialization, rate and abuse limits, secrets exposure, and business-logic
   abuse (replay, race, negative amounts, workflow skipping).
4. Rate each by impact × likelihood, and call out the one or two that are
   genuinely scary versus theoretical.
5. For the top risks, give the specific mitigation and where it belongs in the
   flow (validate and authorize at the boundary, not deep inside).

Be concrete to this feature, not generic.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Audit the codebase for injection & auth flaws
prompts.blurb: Find exploitable vulnerabilities with concrete attack paths.
prompts.summary: Sweeps the code for injection, broken authz/IDOR, SSRF, unsafe deserialization, data exposure, and XSS, showing each as a concrete attack with an example payload and the correct fix.
prompts.body:
Audit this codebase for security vulnerabilities. For anything you flag, show the
concrete attack — the input plus the path it takes — not just a label. Use your
tools to read request handling, queries, auth checks, and any file, network, or
process execution.

Hunt specifically for:
1. Injection: SQL, NoSQL, command, path traversal, template, and header/CRLF — any
   place untrusted input reaches an interpreter, query, filesystem path, or shell
   without proper parameterization or escaping. Quote the line and give an example
   payload.
2. AuthN/AuthZ: missing or bypassable authentication, and — more often missed —
   missing authorization: can a user act on another user's resource (IDOR)? Can
   they escalate privileges or skip a required check?
3. Input trust: unvalidated redirects, SSRF (user-controlled URLs fetched
   server-side), unsafe deserialization, and mass-assignment.
4. Data exposure: secrets in code or logs, sensitive data in responses or errors,
   missing encryption in transit or at rest where it matters.
5. Output handling: XSS from unescaped output into HTML, JS, or attributes.

For each finding: severity, the exploit walk-through, and the correct fix
(parameterize, authorize at the boundary, allowlist, encode on output). Where code
is actually safe but looks risky, say so explicitly.

Don't invent issues to look thorough. If a category is empty, say so and move on. No praise, no restating what the code does.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Dependency & secrets review
prompts.blurb: Check the supply chain and configuration for known-bad inputs.
prompts.summary: Reviews dependencies, committed or leaked secrets, and risky config, names the audit command for your ecosystem, and returns a prioritized issue → risk → exact-fix list.
prompts.body:
Review this project's dependencies, secrets handling, and security-relevant
configuration for risks I can act on. Use your tools to read the dependency
manifest and lockfile, the config, and the code that loads secrets.

Assess:
1. Dependencies: flag packages that are unmaintained, badly outdated, or known to
   carry advisories, and run (or tell me) the authoritative audit command for this
   ecosystem. Distinguish "transitively pulled" from "directly used."
2. Secrets: find any credential, key, or token committed in code, config, or
   history, and any secret that's logged, sent to the client, or baked into a
   build artifact. Recommend the correct handling (env or secret manager,
   rotation, git-history scrubbing if exposed).
3. Configuration: insecure defaults, debug or verbose modes left on, permissive
   CORS, missing security headers, overbroad permissions, and anything safe in dev
   but dangerous in prod.
4. Supply-chain hygiene: are versions pinned and locked? Any unpinned or
   install-time scripts that run arbitrary code?
5. Output a prioritized remediation list: issue → risk → exact fix.

Where judging exploitability needs context not visible in the repo (how a
dependency is used, where config is deployed), state that assumption explicitly
and rate the risk under it rather than over- or under-stating it.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

categories.name: Architecture & Design
categories.blurb: Pressure-test designs, weigh trade-offs honestly, and plan migrations that don't take the system down.

prompts.title: Draft a design doc / RFC
prompts.blurb: Turn a problem into a written design with trade-offs and a recommendation.
prompts.summary: Drafts a design doc — problem, goals and non-goals, constraints, the proposed design and data flow, honest alternatives, trade-offs and risks, and open questions — and pushes on the weak points.
prompts.body:
Help me write a design doc for a problem so reviewers can poke holes in the
thinking, not just the prose. Start by asking me what the problem is and the
constraints (scale, latency, team, deadline, existing systems, hard must-nots) if
I haven't said. Where the design touches this codebase, use your tools to ground
it in what's actually there.

Draft it with these sections, and push on the weak points:
1. Problem and goals: the problem in plain terms, explicit goals, and explicit
   NON-goals. Include the success criteria we'll judge it by.
2. Constraints and assumptions: list them, and mark which assumptions are
   load-bearing (if wrong, the design changes).
3. Proposed design: the approach, the key components and how data flows between
   them, and the main interfaces and contracts. Keep it concrete.
4. Alternatives considered: at least two, each with why it wasn't chosen —
   honestly, not as straw men.
5. Trade-offs and risks: what we're giving up, the failure modes, the operational
   cost, and how we'll observe and roll back. Call out the riskiest part.
6. Open questions: the decisions that still need an owner or more data.

Where my input is thin, ask sharp questions instead of filling gaps with
assumptions. Flag anything over-engineered for the stated scale.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Evaluate trade-offs between approaches
prompts.blurb: Get an honest comparison of candidate approaches that ends in a pick.
prompts.summary: Compares your candidate approaches across the dimensions that matter, makes the trade-offs explicit, and ends in a single recommendation with the assumptions it rests on and the early signal you chose wrong.
prompts.body:
Help me choose between a few approaches with an honest comparison that ends in a
recommendation — not "it depends." Ask me what I'm deciding, the candidate
options, and what matters most (correctness, latency, dev speed, operability,
cost, team familiarity) if I haven't said. Use your tools to check how the options
fit this codebase where that's relevant.

Do this:
1. Restate each option neutrally so we're comparing the same thing, and note any
   I've framed unfairly.
2. Build a comparison across the dimensions that matter (use mine, and add any
   important one I forgot). For each option × dimension, give a concrete
   assessment, not a vague rating — explain the "why" behind it.
3. Make the trade-offs explicit: what each option is genuinely better and worse
   at, and the conditions under which the ranking flips.
4. Identify the deciding factors — the two or three dimensions that should
   actually drive this decision given my priorities.
5. Recommend one, state the assumptions it rests on, and name the early signal
   that would tell us we chose wrong.

If a further option is obviously better than all of mine, say so.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Plan a safe migration / rollout
prompts.blurb: Change a schema, system, or API in production without an outage.
prompts.summary: Produces a staged, reversible expand/contract rollout plan with per-step verification and rollback, a safe batched backfill, and the irreversible point and alerts to watch during cutover.
prompts.body:
Help me plan a production change — a schema, component, or API migration — with no
downtime or data loss, that I can execute and reverse. Ask me for the current
state, the target state, and the constraints (traffic, data volume, downtime
budget, dependents) if I haven't said. Use your tools to read the affected code
and schema.

Produce a staged plan:
1. Define the invariant that must hold throughout (no lost writes, no broken
   reads, consistent data) and the explicit rollback condition.
2. Lay out the expand/contract sequence: add the new path alongside the old,
   dual-write or dual-read or shadow as needed, backfill existing data, switch
   reads, then remove the old path — each step independently deployable and safe
   to pause.
3. For each step, state how to verify success before proceeding and how to roll
   back if it fails (and whether rollback is still safe after the next step).
4. Address data: how to backfill safely (batched, idempotent, resumable), how to
   handle records written during the migration, and how to reconcile and verify.
5. Call out the irreversible point (if any), the riskiest step, and the monitoring
   and alerts to watch during cutover.

Prefer many small reversible steps over one big switch.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

categories.name: Explain & Document
categories.blurb: Understand unfamiliar code fast and turn it into docs the next person can actually use.

prompts.title: Explain unfamiliar code
prompts.blurb: Understand what a part of the codebase does and why, fast.
prompts.summary: Explains a chosen area in layers — purpose, shape and primary path, the non-obvious parts and why, the contract and sharp edges, and what's safe versus load-bearing to change.
prompts.body:
Explain how a part of this codebase works so I understand not just what it does
but why it's shaped that way. Assume I'm a competent engineer new to this code.
Use your tools to read it; if I've named a file, function, or flow, start there,
otherwise pick the most central or load-bearing area and say why you chose it.

Explain in layers, top to bottom:
1. Purpose in one or two sentences: what problem it solves and where it sits in
   the bigger flow (who calls it, what it calls).
2. The shape: the main pieces (functions, types, branches) and how control and
   data move through them. A short step-by-step of the primary path.
3. The non-obvious parts: anything that would make a newcomer pause — a clever
   trick, a workaround, an implicit assumption, an ordering dependency, or a
   subtle edge case being handled. Explain the "why" behind each.
4. The contract and the sharp edges: inputs and outputs, side effects, error
   behavior, and the conditions under which it would misbehave.
5. What I'd want to know before changing it: the parts that look safe to touch and
   the parts that are load-bearing.

If something looks like a bug or a smell rather than intent, flag it separately as
"possible issue, not explanation." Don't invent rationale you can't see — say
"unclear why" when it's unclear.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Write clear docs from the code
prompts.blurb: Produce a README or reference doc grounded in the actual code.
prompts.summary: Writes user-followable docs grounded strictly in the real API — overview, a working getting-started example, a precise reference, common-task recipes, and the gotchas that save a support ticket.
prompts.body:
Draft documentation for a module, API, or library in this codebase, grounded
strictly in the actual code — no invented behavior. Use your tools to read the
public surface (functions, types, endpoints, config, usage); if I haven't named
the target or audience, document the most prominent public surface and state who
you're assuming the reader is.

Produce a draft a real user can follow (in the reply, not as file writes yet):
1. A one-paragraph overview: what this is, what problem it solves, and when to use
   it (and when not to).
2. Getting started: the minimal end-to-end example that actually works,
   copy-pasteable, with the expected result. Base it on the real API.
3. Reference: each public function, endpoint, or option — purpose, parameters
   (with types, units, defaults, required-ness), return or response, errors, and a
   short example. Be precise about edge behavior.
4. Common tasks: a few "how do I X" recipes for what people will actually want to
   do.
5. Gotchas and limits: footguns, constraints, side effects, and anything
   surprising — the stuff that saves a support ticket.

Match the tone and format conventions already used in the project. If the code
doesn't reveal something a doc needs (a default, an error case), mark it as a TODO
or question rather than guessing.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Map an unfamiliar codebase
prompts.blurb: Get oriented in this repo so you know where to make a change.
prompts.summary: Reads the structure and entry points and builds an orientation map — the big-picture flow, which modules own what, the conventions to follow, the danger zones, and where your task likely lives.
prompts.body:
I'm new to this codebase and need to get oriented enough to make a change
confidently. Use your tools to read the directory structure, entry points, build
and config files, and any README, then build me a mental map.

Guide me through orientation:
1. The big picture: what this system does, its main components, and how a request
   or job flows through it end to end. Name the entry point(s).
2. The map: which directories or modules own which responsibility, and where the
   important boundaries are (interfaces, layers, services). Point me at the 5–10
   files worth reading first, in order, and why each.
3. The conventions: the patterns this codebase repeats (error handling, config,
   testing, naming, data access) so a change fits in instead of standing out.
4. The danger zones: the parts that are fragile, heavily depended-on, or
   surprising — where a careless change does the most damage.
5. If I've described a task, tell me where that logic most likely lives and the
   path to trace to confirm it; otherwise, point out the areas a change is most
   likely to touch and what to read to go deeper.

Ground every claim in something you actually read. When you're inferring rather
than confirming, say so and tell me what to open to be sure.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

categories.name: Planning & Delivery
categories.blurb: Turn fuzzy ideas into specs, think out loud with a sharp partner, and write the artifacts shipping needs.

prompts.title: Turn a vague idea into a spec
prompts.blurb: Pin a rough idea down into a buildable spec before building.
prompts.summary: Interrogates a rough idea with the highest-leverage questions, then drafts a spec — problem, users, flows, functional and non-functional requirements, non-goals, acceptance criteria — plus a minimal first slice.
prompts.body:
Help me turn a rough idea into a clear, buildable spec before any code gets
written. Don't write a spec from a vague prompt — interrogate it first. Start by
asking me what the idea is; where it touches this codebase, use your tools to
ground it in what's there.

Then:
1. Play it back: restate what you think I want in one paragraph, and list the
   assumptions you had to make. Mark the ones that materially change the build.
2. Ask the questions that actually matter — the decisions that change scope,
   effort, or design (who's the user, what's the core job, what's explicitly out
   of scope, what are the hard constraints, what does "done" look like). Ask the
   highest-leverage five to eight, not a survey.
3. Once I answer, draft the spec: problem, users, user stories or core flows,
   functional requirements, non-functional requirements (limits, performance,
   security), explicit non-goals, and acceptance criteria.
4. Flag the risky, ambiguous, or expensive parts so we can decide whether to cut
   or de-scope them for a first version.
5. Propose a minimal first slice that delivers the core value, and what to defer.

Bias toward the smallest thing that's genuinely useful. Push back if the idea is
bigger than it needs to be.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Rubber-duck a problem with a sharp partner
prompts.blurb: Think out loud against a partner who challenges your reasoning.
prompts.summary: Acts as a sharp pair-programming partner: reflects your approach, challenges assumptions you haven't verified, asks one focused question at a time, and calls out dead ends instead of letting you waste time.
prompts.body:
Be my pair-programming partner on a problem I'm stuck on. I want pushback and good
questions, not immediate answers. Start by asking me what the problem is, what I've
tried, and my current theory; use your tools to read the relevant code so your
questions are grounded.

How I want you to engage:
1. First, reflect my problem and current approach back to me, and point out any
   assumption I'm treating as fact that I haven't actually verified.
2. Ask one focused question at a time, aimed at the part of my reasoning most
   likely to be wrong, rather than dumping a solution.
3. When I'm clearly heading down a dead end, say so directly and explain why —
   don't let me waste an hour to be polite.
4. If I ask for the answer, give it, but show the reasoning so I can follow it,
   and note where I could have gotten there myself.
5. Periodically summarize what we've established and what's still open, so we don't
   go in circles.

Match my level — assume I'm technical. Prioritize getting me un-stuck and sharper
over sounding agreeable.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.

prompts.title: Write commit messages & changelog entries
prompts.blurb: Turn the current change into clear history and release notes.
prompts.summary: Reads the working diff and writes a clear commit message that explains the why, a user-facing categorized changelog entry where relevant, and a BREAKING CHANGE note when something is incompatible.
prompts.body:
Turn the current change in this repository into a clear commit message (and a
changelog or release-notes entry) that the future reader will thank me for. Use
your tools to read the diff (staged or working changes) and enough surrounding
code to explain the why. If there is no staged or working diff, say so and stop.
Do not invent a commit message.

Produce:
1. A commit message: a concise imperative subject line (around 50 characters, no
   trailing period) that says what the change does, then a body that explains WHY —
   the problem it solves and any context or trade-off — and notes anything risky or
   non-obvious. Reference an issue or ticket if I give one. Match the repo's
   existing commit style.
2. If the change is user-facing, a changelog entry written for users (what changed
   and what it means for them), categorized (Added / Changed / Fixed / Removed /
   Security), not a restatement of the diff.
3. A "BREAKING CHANGE:" note with migration guidance if anything is incompatible.

Keep it honest and specific — no filler like "various improvements." If the change
bundles several unrelated things, point that out and suggest how to split it into
separate commits.

Be concise: findings only, no preamble, no recap of working code.

Do not modify files until I explicitly grant permission. You may propose a plan for file changes if applicable. Wait for the okay before touching anything.
